content: Studies from all diagnostic tests were analyzed to derive a pooled estimate for all technologies. To ensure the pooling of data would yield meaningful results, specific criteria for pooling were established and agreed upon by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) panel before application. Data were also assessed and visualized through direct comparisons of the tests with Xpert® MTB/RIF or other WHO-recommended tests. Criteria for pooling studies on moderate complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) were based on sensitivity, specificity, and preconditions. For inclusion, studies required at least 50 culture-positive tuberculosis (TB) cases and 100 culture-negative TB cases. Two conditions were defined for pooling: 1. Condition 1 (clinical grounds): The pooled estimate of a single test must lie within ±5% of the overall pooled estimate, or within ±2% for stricter criteria. 2. Condition 2 (statistical grounds): The pooled estimate of a single test must lie within the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the overall pooled estimate and within ±10% or ±5% of the overall pooled estimate, depending on the criteria. The certainty of evidence from pooled studies was systematically assessed using PICO questions and the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. GRADE provides an overall quality assessment of evidence and a framework for translating evidence into recommendations. Even observational diagnostic accuracy studies start as high-quality evidence under this approach. The GRADEpro Guideline Development Tool software was used to generate summary tables. Evidence quality was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on five factors: risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and other considerations. Evidence was downgraded by one level for serious issues and by two levels for very serious issues. For PICO 1, which evaluated the use of moderate complexity automated NAATs for detecting pulmonary TB in respiratory samples compared to culture, 29 studies with 13,852 specimens were analyzed. These studies included tests such as Abbott RealTime MTB, FluoroType MTB, FluoroType MTBDR, BD MAX, and cobas MTB. The reference standard was mycobacterial culture. Sixteen studies (55%) had a high or unclear risk of bias due to pre-inclusion specimen testing, convenience sampling, or unreported participant selection methods. The evidence was downgraded for risk of bias. Overall, the certainty of evidence was moderate for sensitivity and high for specificity. Sensitivity ranged from 79% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 60% to 100%. For PICO 2, which assessed the use of moderate complexity automated NAATs for detecting rifampicin resistance compared to culture-based phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST), 18 studies with 2,874 specimens were analyzed. Tests included Abbott RealTime RIF/INH, FluoroType MTBDR, BD MAX, and cobas RIF/INH. The reference standard was phenotypic DST, supplemented by sequencing results to create a composite reference standard. Eight studies (44%) had a high or unclear risk of bias due to unreported participant selection or pre-inclusion specimen testing. Sensitivity for rifampicin resistance detection ranged from 88% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 98% to 100%. Diagnostic accuracy was similar between phenotypic DST and the composite reference standard. For PICO 3, which evaluated the use of moderate complexity automated NAATs for detecting isoniazid resistance compared to culture-based phenotypic DST, 18 studies with 1,758 specimens were analyzed. Tests included Abbott RealTime RIF/INH, FluoroType MTBDR, BD MAX, and cobas MTB-RIF/INH. The reference standard was phenotypic DST, supplemented by sequencing results to create a composite reference standard. Eight studies (44%) had a high or unclear risk of bias due to unreported participant selection or pre-inclusion specimen testing. Sensitivity for isoniazid resistance detection ranged from 58% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 94% to 100%. Diagnostic accuracy was similar between phenotypic DST and the composite reference standard. A systematic review of cost-effectiveness was conducted to evaluate the economic implications of implementing moderate complexity automated NAATs. Four databases (Embase, Medline, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched for studies published between January 2010 and September 2020. No published studies assessing the costs or cost-effectiveness of these tests were identified. One unpublished study comparing two technologies within this category was included. Data from the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) were also reviewed. Time and motion studies conducted in South Africa provided additional insights, but simplifying assumptions (e.g., 50% of laboratory operations dedicated to TB, minimum daily throughput of 24 samples, fixed equipment costs of $100,000, and a 5% annual maintenance cost) may limit generalizability. Cost per test was highly sensitive to testing volume, with significant cost reductions observed at higher volumes. Unit costs stabilized between 5,000 and 10,000 tests per year and became robust above 10,000 tests per year. Optimal equipment placement and multiplexing were identified as key strategies to minimize costs. No studies directly assessed the cost-effectiveness of moderate complexity automated NAATs. Extrapolation was deemed inappropriate due to differences in care standards, operational conditions, testing volumes, and diagnostic accuracy. Economic modeling across various settings is needed to understand cost-effectiveness profiles under different operational criteria. User perspectives on the value, feasibility, usability, and acceptability of diagnostic technologies were also evaluated. A systematic review identified 27 studies, of which 21 were included in the analysis. Most studies were conducted in high TB burden countries, focusing primarily on Xpert MTB/RIF. Semi-structured interviews with clinicians, program officers, laboratory staff, and patient advocates in India, Moldova, and South Africa provided additional insights. These countries were selected based on their high multidrug-resistant TB burden and prior use of index tests in research contexts. Findings emphasized the importance of considering user perspectives to ensure accessibility and effective implementation of diagnostic technologies.
